haiku-low.q1: Pages of 500 products ordered by product id ascending, using keyset cursor after_id. Only one page request is in flight at a time, so no parallel fetching.
haiku-low.q2: In sync_state in SQLite, as after_id. It is advanced in the same transaction that saves the page's rows to products_staging, so page and cursor always agree.
haiku-low.q3: After all pages are saved, the client replays every change with change_seq above start_seq into staging. Commit-ordered change_seq means no later edit is missed; stale changes are skipped.
haiku-low.q4: The server returns HTTP 410 with resync_required. The client leaves products untouched, restarts the full download with a fresh start_seq, and swaps it in when complete.
haiku-low.q5: Staging is emptied, a new start_seq is taken, pages and catch-up fill products_staging. One transaction in step 8 renames it to products, replacing the old catalogue; reps see the old one until then.
haiku-low.q6: App launch or return to foreground starts it. It runs at most once every 15 minutes, measured from last_incremental_at stored in SQLite, only when phase is none and last_seq exists.
haiku-low.q7: It retries the same request, at most 5 attempts total, waiting 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds. After the fifth failure it stops until the next trigger and keeps saved progress.
haiku-low.q8: It finishes the in-flight request, saves it, then stops before the next one. It resumes from the saved cursor when Wi-Fi returns, or at next launch or foreground.
haiku-low.q9: It applies the change only if no local row exists or its change_seq is greater than the row's change_seq. Otherwise it skips the change.
haiku-low.q10: It starts from last_seq in sync_state, the live catalogue position. last_seq advances after each batch, in the same transaction that applies that batch.
haiku-low.q11: It reads product changes ordered by change_seq from Postgres, indexed on change_seq. Deletes appear as tombstones, rows with deleted = true kept for 7 days.

sonnet.q1: Keyset pagination: GET /catalogue/full?after=<product_id>, 500 non-deleted products per page ordered by product id ascending (about 800 pages), with next_after as the cursor (null on last page). Only one page request is ever in flight, so no parallel fetching.
sonnet.q2: In the single-row SQLite sync_state table, as after_id. Each page's rows are written to products_staging and after_id is set to next_after in the same SQLite transaction, so a page is either fully saved with the cursor advanced or not saved at all.
sonnet.q3: At start the client stores the server's current change_seq as start_seq. After all pages are saved, it fetches every change after start_seq (catch-up, via /changes, repeated while has_more) and applies them to the staging table. Edits committed after start_seq have higher change_seq so appear in the changes; earlier ones were already visible when pages were read. Deletes arrive as tombstones. Changes are applied only if newer than the local row's change_seq.
sonnet.q4: The server (which tracks oldest_valid_seq, the highest change_seq of any purged tombstone) answers HTTP 410 with resync_required if since < oldest_valid_seq. The client does not retry it; it goes to step 10: leaves products untouched and restarts a full download (step 3, then steps 4 to 8).
sonnet.q5: Step 3 empties products_staging and sets a fresh start_seq; steps 4 to 8 download pages and catch up into products_staging while the old products table stays in use. The new catalogue becomes the one read at step 8's swap, a single SQLite transaction that drops products and renames products_staging to products, which is the only point where the old catalogue is replaced.
sonnet.q6: App launch or return to foreground, at most once every 15 minutes (compared with last_incremental_at stored in SQLite, set when the sync starts, so failed attempts count). It needs phase = none and a last_seq, runs on any network, and does not run during a full download or catch-up.
sonnet.q7: Retries the same request: at most 5 attempts in total, waiting 2 s, 4 s, 8 s, then 16 s between them. After the fifth failure it stops and waits for the next trigger, keeping everything saved and continuing from the saved cursor or position.
sonnet.q8: The client finishes the request in flight, saves it as in step 4 (or 7), then stops before making the next request. sync_state already holds phase and after_id/catchup_seq, so nothing extra is stored. It resumes from the saved cursor when Wi-Fi returns (network-change callback) or at the next launch or foreground.
sonnet.q9: It compares change_seq: the change is applied only if no local row exists or its change_seq is greater than the local row's change_seq. Otherwise it is skipped, so applying the same change twice is harmless.
sonnet.q10: It starts from last_seq in sync_state: GET /catalogue/changes?since=<last_seq>, repeated while has_more is true. last_seq is advanced after each batch, in the same transaction that applies that batch.
sonnet.q11: It reads from Postgres only, using change_seq (a global, strictly increasing sequence stamped on every insert, update or delete at commit), returning up to 1,000 changes with change_seq > since ordered by change_seq ascending, with indexes on change_seq and product id. Deletes are represented as tombstones: the row kept with deleted = true for 7 days and then purged.
